title: Find where a program keeps its configuration files
summary: Most programs keep their settings in your home folder, in ~/.config or in a hidden dot-file, or for all users in /etc. These commands search those places by the program's name.

aliases.text: where does a program store its settings
find config folder of a program
where are app settings saved linux
where is the config file of a program
где конфиг файл программы в linux
где appdata в linux как в windows

prerequisites: You know the name of the program, or part of it, for example bash or nano.

steps.explain: Check that the program is installed. The output is the path of its command, or nothing if the program is not installed.

placeholders.name: PROGRAM_NAME
placeholders.description: Part of the program's name, as you type it in the terminal.

steps.expect: A path such as /usr/bin/<PROGRAM_NAME>, or no output if the program is not installed.

steps.explain: Look for folders in your personal settings folder ~/.config whose name contains the program name. Many programs keep their settings there. If ~/.config is missing, the error No such file or directory appears; go on to the next steps.

placeholders.name: PROGRAM_NAME
placeholders.description: Part of the program's name, as you type it in the terminal.

steps.expect: A path such as /home/<you>/.config/<PROGRAM_NAME>. No output means no folder matches in ~/.config.

steps.explain: Look in /etc, the system-wide settings folder. Programs that apply to all users keep their main settings there.

placeholders.name: PROGRAM_NAME
placeholders.description: Part of the program's name, as you type it in the terminal.

steps.expect: Paths that start with /etc/, such as /etc/<PROGRAM_NAME>/ or /etc/<PROGRAM_NAME>.conf. No output means /etc has no matching file.

steps.explain: Look in your home folder for hidden dot-files of the program, such as .bashrc or .nanorc. Hidden files do not show in a plain ls, so this search finds them.

placeholders.name: PROGRAM_NAME
placeholders.description: Part of the program's name, as you type it in the terminal.

steps.expect: Hidden files such as /home/<you>/.<PROGRAM_NAME>rc, or no output if none exist.

warnings: Files in /etc belong to the system. Reading them is safe, but changing them needs sudo, and you should copy the file first.
